## IAM-Atlas v2.1: a reference built and checked as a calibrated map

IAM-Atlas v2.1 joins two bodies of method that developed apart. Genomics built the assays, the reference cell types and the deconvolution that read a cell's methylation; cosmology built the statistics that turn many noisy, differently calibrated scans of one faint signal into a single map with a stated uncertainty at every point. Each field built its toolkit because its data demanded it, and neither had reason to borrow the other's.

The atlas applies the second toolkit to the first field's data, because both problems are the same kind of problem: a faint signal at hundreds of thousands of positions, read through instruments that each carry their own offset, where the value at each position is only as useful as its stated uncertainty.

This is not a bigger table built for the sake of putting more cells in one place. A blended 79-cell atlas with MCMC posteriors would be interesting, but not new. What is new is how it was built and how it was checked: the way cosmologists build and check a map of the sky. That is what we mean by the information physics of the methylome, and every tool below is something a geneticist can use in their own work, not only in ours.

### The tools, in IAM-Atlas v2.1

| tool | in cosmology | in IAM-Atlas v2.1 | IAM-Atlas's unique capability |
|---|---|---|---|
| **One map from many instruments** | Planck's sky maps were made by fitting every scan from every detector together, with each scan's own offset fitted alongside the sky (destriping). | 21 sources, arrays and sequencing from many laboratories, are fitted together in one hierarchical model. Each laboratory's offset is fitted apart from the cells, so the same cell measured by two laboratories becomes one cell, not two. | One reference across laboratories and platforms, instead of one table per laboratory. |
| **The whole posterior, sampled (MCMC)** | Cosmologists estimate the parameters of the universe from the microwave background by Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, which returns every answer with its full uncertainty. | The No-U-Turn sampler fitted 813,951 array sites in 700 blocks. Every site and cell carries its best value, its 95 % range, the number of observations behind it, and the posterior draws themselves (100 per block): 60,687,175 measured cell-site values. | An error bar on every reference value, and draws that carry the reference's own uncertainty into any deconvolution or marker search built on it. |
| **A convergence certificate at every site** | No cosmological chain is reported without its Gelman-Rubin statistic (R-hat), the check that the sampler has settled. | R-hat and the effective sample size are stored for every site and cell. 0.42 % of values sit at R-hat 1.01 or above, and the whole fit had 13 divergent transitions in 700 blocks. Flagged values are kept, with the flag. | You know which reference values to trust before you use them. |
| **Masks, never filling** | Where the galaxy hides the sky, cosmologists mask it rather than paint it over. | Where a cell's sources never measured a site, the value is left blank (not measured), never imputed, and the count of observations sits beside every value. | No invented reference value slips into a deconvolution. |
| **Sample variance: the next person, not only the average** | Cosmic variance is the spread a different sky would show: how well the average is known is a different question from how much one realization varies. | The fit separates how well each cell's average is known from how much a new person's cell varies around it (the donor spread), at every site. | A range for a new person's cells, not just an error on the mean. Our deconvolution tool already reads it. |
| **Cross-calibrating two instruments** | Planck's maps were compared with WMAP's on the same sky, and a calibration difference between the two telescopes was traced and resolved. | Arrays and sequencing measure the same mark in two different ways, and the two do not agree along a straight line. On 767,672 sites measured both ways in the same 17 cell types, the relation turned out to be S-shaped, differing by up to 0.08 at the low end. IAM-Atlas v2.1 translates between the two with one measured curve that always stays between 0 and 1, tested on planted data before the fit. | Array and sequencing data read against one reference, on one scale. A conversion along a straight line carries an error of up to 0.08; IAM-Atlas v2.1 carries the measured curve itself. |
| **Blind analysis and sealed bars** | Modern microwave-background and dark-energy analyses are blinded: the tests are fixed before anyone sees the answer. | Every commissioning bar was sealed before the atlas existed, on held-out laboratories that share no GEO contributor with any source, and each use was scored once. | A reference whose claims were fixed before the data could flatter it. |
| **Tested on held-out skies** | A map earns trust on data that played no part in making it. | Held-out cells from independent laboratories, the blind sites of the tissue tests, and head-to-heads against the two published reference atlases of human cell types, one built on arrays and one on sequencing, on the jobs each was built for: three of three bars met against each. | Evidence on independent samples, not on the training data. |

### The tools, complementary additions, ready or in progress

| tool | in cosmology | in IAM-Atlas v2.1 | IAM-Atlas's unique capability |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Noise maps from the posterior draws** | Planck released noise simulations alongside its sky maps, so others could tell signal from noise. | Maps of where the atlas is unsure. Built: every cell's uncertainty map (the width of each value's 95 % range, pixel by pixel), on every cell page. Next: noise maps drawn from the fit's own posterior draws, published with the fit. | See where a reference can and cannot be leaned on, site by site. |
| **The sky sphere, with masks and apodization** | The sky is stored on the HEALPix sphere, with masks and smooth mask edges (apodization) so the edges do not create false structure. | Every site of the atlas at one fixed place on an equal-area HEALPix sphere, set by its genome address, so every cell and every sample share one map site for site. What the sphere gives over a flat map: every pixel the same area, so no part of the genome is stretched; no edges or seams; genome neighbors share small patches, so clustered change shows as patches and scattered noise as speckle; and the sky's masks apply unchanged. A spectrum on this map measures order along the genome's address, which is bookkeeping, not the order a cell holds: spectra belong to the information sphere. Built: all 79 cells, unmeasured pixels masked, and the Globe Explorer, where a reader turns every cell, Met-A's purified-array reference and example samples (https://hmahaffeyges.github.io/IAM-Validation/atlas/sphere.html), and every report's own globe, which shows the sample against its healthy reference on the same pixels. The layout is the genome's address; the map of the order itself, where a site's place comes from how it behaves, is the information sphere (DEV-SPHERE-01, in development). Next: apodized masks once statistics are computed on the maps. | A picture of healthy order across all 79 cells at once. |
| **The guidebook** | Every tool above, with its origin and history in cosmology. | How each tool applies to the methylome, how it differs from what geneticists use now (such as the bootstrap), and its limits. Built: the short form, the tools on this page. Next: the full guidebook. | An instruction manual for the new tools. |

### The tools, on the horizon

| tool | in cosmology | in IAM-Atlas v2.1 | IAM-Atlas's unique capability |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Two half-atlases and null maps** | Planck's half-mission split: two maps from two halves of the data; their difference must be pure noise. | The atlas refitted on two sealed halves of every cell's donors; half A minus half B is a noise map with no signal in it. | A direct test of the atlas's stated noise, and noise-free cross-spectra. |
| **Power spectra, simulations and higher-order statistics** | Masked power spectra with shuffled nulls, end-to-end simulations that measure the pipeline's own transfer function, and three-point and Minkowski statistics of the residuals. | The same statistics on the atlas maps, each against its simulated null, and the cross-site covariance of healthy donors. | Structure in healthy methylation that a table of means cannot show. |

**What is commissioned.** IAM-Atlas v2.1 is commissioned use by use, each on its own sealed test: as the reference for cortical neurons, lung bronchus epithelium and naive CD4 T cells; as the source of the blind sites in the colon and lung tissue tests; and, read by the IAM-Deconvolver, for the blood-cell shares of neutrophils, monocytes, CD4 and CD8 T cells (mean share error 0.016 on mixtures from a laboratory the atlas never saw). Every one of its 813,951 sites is keyed both to its array probe and to its CpG position in the published sequencing atlas, so array and sequencing tools open the same atlas.

*Methods built to map a faint signal on a sphere, applied to the cell, because the same statistics serve both records.*

# IAM-Atlas v2.1: compact copy

The fitted atlas (2026-10-16): 79 cell types, 813,951 array sites, from the Bayesian fit of record `../../doors/DEV_ATLAS_V21_01.md`.
**Commissioned use by use** (`../../doors/COMMISSIONING_NOTE_ATLAS_V21.md`): three cell reference profiles and the blind sites of the colon and lung tissue tests; every other use is labeled development until it passes its own sealed test.

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `sites.parquet` | every site id, in the row order of the tables below |
| `mu_part1-3.parquet` | best estimate (posterior mean) per site and cell; columns are the cells, in the source atlases' exact names |
| `mu_lo_part1-3.parquet`, `mu_hi_part1-3.parquet` | the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles (the 95 % range of the cell's average) |
| `donor_sd_part1-3.parquet` | the fit's person-to-person spread of each cell at each site (posterior mean of the donor SD); a new person's cell varies this much around the average |
| `sites_sequencing_key.parquet` | the same sites in sequencing coordinates: Illumina probe ID, the CpG index of the published sequencing atlas's .beta files (Loyfer et al. 2023, GSE186458; wgbstools numbering, 1-based; all 813,951 sites keyed, none shared), and the manifest chromosome and position (hg19). Join it to any table above to open the atlas in sequencing tools at these sites |
| `compact_manifest.json` | each file's size and SHA-256 |

**Scope:** v2.1 is an array-scale reference, one value per site at about 814,000 array CpGs; it holds no molecule-level (read-level) markers.

Values are stored as round(value x 10000) in unsigned 16-bit integers: value = stored / 10000 (exact to 4 decimals); **65535 = not measured**.
The 79 cells are split into three files in alphabetical order so every file stays under GitHub's 100 MB limit; join the parts side by side.

Checked 2026-10-16: every file matches its checksum, and on three cells at every site the copy differs from the full atlas by at most 0.00005
(the rounding). Made by `../../doors/data/DEV_ATLAS_V21_01/export_compact_v21.py` (rounding only). The full atlas file (2.4 GB, with donor
spread, R-hat and ESS per site) and the 100 posterior draws per block (24 GB) are public in Zenodo record [10.5281/zenodo.23422688](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23422688)
(ten bundles of 70 blocks, each file checked by `output_manifest_v21.json`); the fitted atlas is record [10.5281/zenodo.23441999](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23441999).

```python
import pandas as pd
sites = pd.read_parquet("sites.parquet").cpg
mu = pd.concat([pd.read_parquet(f"mu_part{n}.parquet") for n in (1, 2, 3)], axis=1)
mu.index = sites; mu = mu.where(mu != 65535) / 10000
```
